Accuracy.description:
How the feature's coordinates relate to the thing it names.

| accuracy | Pack point |
| --- | --- |
| `rooftop` | the point of an address or POI (`point`) |
| `interpolated` | a house number placed along a range or between neighbours (`estimated`) |
| `street` | a point on a street or range line (`representative_point`, reverse `street`) |
| `centroid` | the centre of a drawn way or relation (`centroid`) |
| `approximate` | a node or derived point standing for something larger: a place node, a postcode |

Accuracies order from the most precise.

Address.description:
Address parts as the record states them. A part the record leaves out is
absent, never filled in from the areas around it: those are the
`context`.

areas.description:
The areas below the locality the address names, outermost first
(`addr:suburb`, `addr:quarter`, `addr:neighbourhood`).

place.description: `addr:place`: what the house number is on where there is no street.

Attribution.description: The licence every answer is given under.

Common.description:
What a feature is, where it lies and where it comes from: everything both
directions say about an answer.

Not a response type of its own. It is flattened into
[`ForwardProperties`] and [`ReverseProperties`], which add the one field
their direction ranks by, so that both are one flat object on the wire.

address.description: The address parts the record itself states, and only those.

context.description: The areas the record lies in, from the Pack's boundaries.

label.description: One line to show, the name followed by where it is.

name.description:
The thing itself: a POI's or place's name, a street's name, or an
address's house number and street (`12 King Street West`).

record_id.description: Row of the record in this Pack. Not stable across Pack builds.

Context.description:
The areas a record lies in, one per tier: the admin areas most specific
first, then the place area.

The `sub` tiers carry the levels a country maps between the conventional
ones. Germany mapping three `state_district` levels used to mean two of
them were dropped from every German address; they are now the district
and its subdistrict. The field is absent where a country does not map
that depth, as every field here already is, so a reader of the
conventional tiers alone is unaffected.

place.description:
A named area outside the admin levels, mostly an island. It can be
smaller than a locality or larger than a region (Honshu).

id.description: The area's source id, as a feature's `id`.

ForwardCollection.description:
A forward answer: `/search` and `/autocomplete`.

Forward and reverse answers are the same GeoJSON FeatureCollection, best
or most precise first, differing only in what `geocoding` says and in the
one ranking field each feature carries. Each direction is written out
rather than shared through a generic, because a generic reached through a
type alias is transparent to the schema generator: it produced one
`FeatureCollection` component for both directions and pointed `/search`
and `/reverse` at it, so the published contract described each endpoint
with the other's fields. The duplication here is what makes the generated
schemas distinct and true. The construction logic is still shared, by
[`common`] and the builders below.

geocoding.description: What was asked, the contract version and the data attribution.

ForwardFeature.description: One forward answer: a record of the Pack, or a house number placed on one.

query.description:
The query text as received, trimmed, with each run of whitespace
written as one space.

confidence.description:
The chance this answer is the address or place the query asks for,
from 0 to 1, comparable across queries: of the answers given 0.8,
about eight in ten are right. It is calibrated per Pack, by
`geocode calibrate` on held-out addresses, and is absent from every
answer of a Pack that has not been calibrated. A `fallback` is no
answer to what the query asks for, and its confidence is 0.

fallback.description:
Present, and `true`, when the feature is no match of what the query
asks for but the finest area it names that the Pack holds: its
postcode, a place it names, its region or its country. It is given
only when nothing more precise was found, and `layer` and `accuracy`
say how coarse it is. Absent from every other answer.

score.description:
Text relevance: higher is better, comparable only within one answer.

It orders the features of one response and nothing else. It is not a
probability, not a quality score, and not comparable between queries
or between Packs — two answers' scores say nothing about each other.
To judge how good a single answer is, read `confidence`, or
`accuracy` and `layer`, which mean the same thing in every response.

ForwardProperties.description:
A forward feature's properties: the common fields, and the text relevance
`/search` and `/autocomplete` rank by.

ForwardResult.description: One item's result: `response` when it succeeded, `error` when it failed.

status.description: The status `GET` would have answered this item with.

address.description:

town or postcode.

limit.description: How many candidates to consider before picking the best.

locality.description: The town or city the address is in.

Layer.description:
Every record layer. Place layers are the context layers used to describe
where an address is.

ObjectType.description:
What a record's source object is: an OSM node, way or relation, or a row
of an imported address dataset such as OpenAddresses.

Problem.description:
The error body, as the contract describes it.

A schema-only mirror of [`crate::http::problem::Problem`], whose fields are
private so that nothing but its constructors can build one.
`problem_schema_matches_the_rendered_body` holds the two together.

What went wrong, in prose. Absent on a 500, which never explains
itself to a client.

error_code.description: The stable value to branch on.

invalid_params.description:

parameters.

type.description:
A URI identifying the problem type. `about:blank` while the problem

Source.description:

Version.description:
The contract version. It changes only when a field changes meaning or

info.description:
Search, autocomplete and reverse geocoding served from a single binary Pack built from OpenStreetMap extracts.

Every answer is one GeoJSON FeatureCollection, so a response drops straight into a map library. Forward answers carry a `score`, and a calibrated `confidence` once the Pack has been calibrated; reverse answers carry a `distance_m`. Nothing else differs between them.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem documents served as `application/problem+json`. Branch on `error_code`, which is a closed set; `title` and `detail` are prose and may be reworded.

get.summary: Suggest places as a query is typed.

get.description:
For callers who hold a street address, a town and a postcode in separate
fields and would otherwise have to paste them into one string and hope the
parser pulls them apart again. The street address is searched on its own
and hits are kept only where they fit the locality, region and postcode
given, so a town in the address cannot outrank the street.

This is the lookup `geocode batch` runs per row, over HTTP.

A house number the data lacks is placed between its neighbours
(`accuracy` `interpolated`) or, failing that, answered with its street
(`accuracy` `street`). A street answers a given postcode only where
postcode data confirms it. The answer is never another house: a flat
written "10/1367" is found as itself or by 1367, never as house 10.

The answer is the same FeatureCollection every other route returns, with
at most one feature: `features` holds the one match, or is empty when
nothing fits. `geocoding.query` is the rewrite that matched, which is not
always the address as it was sent.

post.description:
The body is a JSON array of up to 1000 items, each taking the parameters
`GET /geocode` takes, plus an optional `id` echoed in its result. The
request's own query-string parameters apply to every item, and an item's
own fields override them: `?country=CA` scopes every item to Canada.
`QUERY` takes the same body and answers the same: `POST` is for clients
that cannot send `QUERY`.

Each result's `response` is exactly what `GET` returns for its item, and
its `error` the Problem `GET` would return. Results are in input order,
one per item, and a bad item never fails the batch.
